o: Synapses in the olfactory tract

Olfactory filaments synapse with the mitral cells of the olfactory bulb.
Mitral cell axons then run back in the olfactory tract. (Last's p. 589)
Relays in the thalamus before reaching the cortex

Smell is the one sense with no thalamic relay on the way to its cortex (the uncus).
There are only two neurons from receptor to cortex. (Last's p. 586)
Consists of about 100 filaments on each side

There are nearly 20 filaments on each side.
They are bundles of unmyelinated axons of the olfactory receptor cells. (Last's p. 629)
Has filaments that pierce dura and arachnoid at the cribriform plate

The filaments pass through the cribriform plate, piercing dura and arachnoid to reach the bulb.
This is how a fracture here can cause CSF rhinorrhoea and anosmia. (Last's p. 568, 629)
Is about 3 cm long in the orbit

The orbital part is about 3 cm long and slightly wavy, allowing eye movement.
It is longer than the distance from optic canal to eyeball. (Last's p. 512)
Joins the eyeball at the posterior pole

It joins the sclera 3 mm medial to the posterior pole.
The optic disc is therefore nasal to the macula. (Last's p. 512)
Has its posterior orbital part supplied by the central artery of the retina

The posterior 2 cm is supplied by the ophthalmic artery; the central artery supplies the anterior 1 cm.
The central artery enters the nerve about 1 cm behind the eye. (Last's p. 512)
Is myelinated by Schwann cells

The optic nerve is a CNS tract, myelinated by oligodendrocytes.
It is wrapped in all three meninges, with subarachnoid space round it. (Last's)
Passes through the superior orbital fissure as a single trunk

It divides in the cavernous sinus wall into lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves.
These three branches pass through the fissure separately. (Last's p. 567)
Has a nasociliary branch that passes within the tendinous ring

Nasociliary passes through the ring, with III and VI.
It then crosses above the optic nerve to the medial wall. (Last's p. 630)
Has a lacrimal branch carrying its own secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion

Secretomotor fibres for the lacrimal gland come from the pterygopalatine ganglion via the zygomatic nerve.
The otic ganglion supplies the parotid. (Last's p. 450, 451)
Has a frontal branch that passes above the tendinous ring

Frontal and lacrimal nerves (with IV) pass above the ring, outside the muscle cone.
Frontal runs forward on levator palpebrae superioris. (Last's p. 513-4, 451, 508)

questions.s: Branches of the nasociliary nerve include:
o: Long ciliary nerves

Two or three long ciliary nerves carry sensation from the eyeball, including the cornea.
They also carry sympathetic fibres to dilator pupillae. (Last's p. 632)
The sensory root of the ciliary ganglion

Sensory fibres pass through the ciliary ganglion without relaying.
They reach the eye in the short ciliary nerves. (Last's p. 630)
The anterior ethmoidal nerve

It supplies the anterior nasal cavity and ends as the external nasal nerve on the nose.
Its skin territory explains Hutchinson's sign in ophthalmic zoster. (Last's p. 632)
The infratrochlear nerve

It supplies skin of the medial eyelids and side of the nose.
It runs below the trochlea of superior oblique. (Last's p. 632)
Leaves the skull through the foramen ovale

It leaves through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa.
The mandibular nerve uses the foramen ovale. (Last's p. 654)
Supplies the muscles of mastication

The maxillary nerve is purely sensory.
The mandibular nerve supplies the muscles of mastication. (Last's)
Lies in the medial wall of the cavernous sinus

It lies in the lower part of the lateral wall.
The internal carotid and VI lie within the sinus. (Last's p. 631)
Continues into the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure as the infraorbital nerve

It deviates laterally for about 1 cm in the fissure, then runs forward in the infraorbital groove.
It emerges on the face at the infraorbital foramen. (Last's p. 511)
The posterior superior alveolar nerves arise in the pterygopalatine fossa

They run down on the back of the maxilla to the molar teeth.
They give a gingival branch to the buccal gum. (Last's p. 633)
The zygomatic nerve carries secretomotor fibres towards the lacrimal gland

Postganglionic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion travel in it.
They join the lacrimal nerve through a communicating branch. (Last's p. 635-6)
The greater palatine nerve supplies the gums and mucosa of the hard palate

It runs down the greater palatine canal to the hard palate.
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the area behind the incisors. (Last's p. 632-3)
The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the incisor teeth

It leaves the infraorbital nerve in the floor of the orbit and supplies the premolars and the anterior buccal root of the first molar.
The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the canine and incisors. (Last's)
Gives the nerve to mylohyoid before entering the mandibular foramen

The nerve to mylohyoid pierces the sphenomandibular ligament and runs in its groove.
It supplies mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric. (Last's p. 460-462)
Is a branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve

It is a branch of the posterior division, with the lingual and auriculotemporal nerves.
The anterior division is mainly motor, plus the buccal nerve. (Last's p. 459)
Supplies the lingual gum of the lower teeth

The lingual gum is supplied by the lingual nerve.
The inferior alveolar supplies the lower teeth and, via the mental nerve, the lower lip and chin. (Last's p. 477)
Supplies the anterior belly of digastric through its mental branch

The mental nerve is sensory to the lip and chin.
Anterior digastric is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid. (Last's p. 634)

questions.s: Concerning branches of the mandibular nerve:
o: The buccal nerve supplies buccinator

The buccal nerve is sensory to the cheek skin and mucosa.
Buccinator is supplied by the facial nerve. (Last's p. 460-462)
The auriculotemporal nerve carries fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion

It carries postganglionic fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid.
The pterygopalatine ganglion supplies lacrimal, nasal and palatal glands. (Last's p. 450, 451)
The masseteric nerve arises from the posterior division

Masseteric, deep temporal, lateral pterygoid and buccal nerves come from the anterior division.
The posterior division is mainly sensory. (Last's p. 460-462)
The nervus spinosus arises from the trunk before it divides

Nervus spinosus and the nerve to medial pterygoid arise from the undivided trunk.
The nervus spinosus returns through the foramen spinosum to supply dura. (Last's p. 633)
Leaves the facial nerve above the geniculate ganglion

It leaves the facial nerve in the facial canal about 6 mm above the stylomastoid foramen.
All its fibres belong to the nervus intermedius. (Last's p. 636)
Crosses the tympanic membrane over the neck of the malleus

It passes forward across the pars flaccida and the neck of the malleus, under mucous membrane.
It can be damaged in middle-ear surgery. (Last's p. 636)
Leaves the skull through the foramen ovale

It leaves at the medial end of the petrotympanic fissure.
It then grooves the medial side of the spine of the sphenoid. (Last's p. 460-462)
Joins the lingual nerve about 2 cm below the skull

It joins the lingual nerve just above the lower border of lateral pterygoid.
Through it, taste fibres reach the anterior tongue. (Last's p. 634, 636)
Carries preganglionic fibres to the otic ganglion

Its secretomotor fibres relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion.
The lesser petrosal nerve (from IX) goes to the otic ganglion. (Last's p. 635-6)
Arises from the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen

It leaves the geniculate ganglion.
It runs forward and medially at a 45° slant through the petrous bone. (Last's p. 635-6)
Joins the deep petrosal nerve at the foramen ovale

They join at the foramen lacerum to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
The deep petrosal is sympathetic, from the internal carotid plexus. (Last's p. 571)
Can cause a temporary facial paresis if pulled during extradural surgery

Traction may cause bleeding or oedema at the geniculate ganglion, pressing on the facial nerve.
It lies between the two dural layers in the middle cranial fossa. (Last's p. 635-6)
Gives the nerve to stapedius in the facial canal

The nerve to stapedius arises in the descending part of the canal.
Its loss causes hyperacusis. (Last's p. 635)
Emerges from the brainstem at the upper border of the pons

The facial nerve and nervus intermedius emerge at the lower border of the pons (pontomedullary junction).
They lie medial to VIII in the cerebellopontine angle. (Last's p. 609)
Passes deep to the retromandibular vein in the parotid

The facial nerve is the most superficial of the structures in the parotid.
The retromandibular vein lies deep to it, and the external carotid deeper still. (Last's p. 452)
Supplies the posterior belly of digastric through the chorda tympani

It supplies posterior digastric and stylohyoid by direct branches below the stylomastoid foramen.
The chorda tympani carries taste and secretomotor fibres only. (Last's p. 636)
Has about 18 000 fibres in its cochlear part

The cochlear nerve has about 30 000 fibres; the vestibular about 18 000.
Both pass through the internal acoustic meatus. (Last's p. 637)
Causes deafness in the opposite ear when one auditory cortex is damaged

Each cochlea is bilaterally represented in the cortex.
So a unilateral cortical lesion does not cause deafness. (Last's p. 586)
Has its vestibular and cochlear nuclei combined into one nucleus

The vestibular and cochlear nuclei are separate.
Cochlear nuclei lie on the inferior cerebellar peduncle; vestibular nuclei lie under the floor of the fourth ventricle. (Last's p. 609)
Has vestibular nuclei beneath the vestibular area of the fourth ventricle

The vestibular area at the lateral angle of the floor overlies the vestibular nuclei.
It extends into both pons and medulla. (Last's p. 609)
Includes fibres crossing in the trapezoid body at the pontomedullary junction

The trapezoid body is the transverse decussation of fibres from the cochlear nuclei.
Its fibres turn up as the lateral lemniscus. (Last's p. 609)
Includes the lateral lemniscus ending in the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate body

Lateral lemniscal fibres end in these nuclei for auditory reflexes and relay.
Cell stations connect to the extraocular nuclei via the medial longitudinal bundle. (Last's p. 637)
Reaches the transverse temporal gyri through the auditory radiation

The medial geniculate body sends the auditory radiation to areas 41 and 42.
These lie mostly hidden in the lateral sulcus. (Last's p. 586)
Relays in the medial geniculate body of the midbrain tectum

The medial geniculate body is part of the thalamus (metathalamus).
The inferior colliculus is the tectal relay. (Last's p. 595-6)
The mesencephalic nucleus carries pain from the face

The mesencephalic nucleus serves proprioception, mainly from muscles of mastication.
Its cells are the only primary sensory cell bodies inside the CNS. (Last's p. 615)
The spinal nucleus extends down into the upper cervical cord

It continues to about C2, merging with the substantia gelatinosa.
So upper cervical lesions can affect facial pain sensation. (Last's p. 603-604)
The main sensory nucleus lies in the medulla

The main (principal) sensory nucleus lies in the pons, beside the motor nucleus.
It serves touch. (Last's p. 635)
Facial pain and temperature fibres relay in the spinal nucleus

They descend in the spinal tract before synapsing in the spinal nucleus.
This is why lateral medullary syndrome gives ipsilateral facial analgesia. (Last's p. 613)
Has secretomotor fibres from the superior salivary nucleus

Its secretomotor fibres come from the inferior salivary nucleus.
The superior salivary nucleus belongs to the facial nerve. (Last's p. 637)
Supplies all muscles of the pharynx

Its only muscle is stylopharyngeus.
The other pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 637)
Sends parasympathetic fibres to the parotid in the greater petrosal nerve

They travel in the tympanic branch and lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion.
Then via the auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid. (Last's p. 456-7)
Carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

Taste fibres from the posterior tongue end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
So do afferents from the carotid sinus and body. (Last's p. 637)
Has a dorsal nucleus with secretomotor cells for glands, including the stomach

The dorsal nucleus contains motor cells for cardiac and visceral muscle and secretomotor cells for glands.
Its afferent cells belong to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius. (Last's p. 610)
Has its branchial motor fibres coming from the dorsal nucleus

Branchial motor fibres to the pharynx and larynx come from the nucleus ambiguus.
The dorsal nucleus is visceral. (Last's p. 637)
Has only about 10% afferent fibres in the abdomen

About 90% of abdominal vagal fibres are afferent.
They serve reflex activity rather than conscious sensation. (Last's p. 638)
Has an auricular branch supplying the skin of the whole auricle

The auricular branch supplies a small area: part of the external acoustic meatus and skin over the mastoid.
Most of the auricle is supplied by the great auricular and auriculotemporal nerves. (Last's p. 638)
Has an external branch supplying posterior cricoarytenoid

The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid.
Posterior cricoarytenoid, like all other intrinsic muscles, is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal. (Last's p. 638)
Has an internal branch piercing the thyrohyoid membrane

The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery.
It runs under the mucosa of the piriform fossa. (Last's p. 638)
Hooks round the subclavian artery

That is the right recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The superior laryngeal nerve passes down deep to both carotid arteries. (Last's p. 638)
Has an internal branch supplying mucosa above the vocal folds

The internal laryngeal nerve supplies mucosa down to the vocal folds.
Below the folds the recurrent laryngeal takes over. (Last's p. 638)
Leaves the cord and exits through the jugular foramen without entering the skull

Its spinal root ascends through the foramen magnum into the skull first.
It then leaves through the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 572)
Supplies trapezius alone

It supplies both sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
C3 and C4 give mainly sensory (proprioceptive) fibres to these muscles. (Last's p. 639)
Runs deep to the floor of the posterior triangle

It runs within the investing fascia forming the roof of the triangle.
That superficial position makes it easy to damage. (Last's p. 439)
Is at risk in lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle

It crosses the triangle superficially and often runs among the lymph nodes.
Damage causes trapezius weakness and shoulder drop. (Last's p. 438, 442, 462)
Oculomotor nerve about 24 000

The oculomotor nerve has about 24 000 fibres.
They sweep through the red nucleus and substantia nigra on the way out. (Last's p. 630)
Trochlear nerve about 3400

The trochlear is the smallest cranial nerve, with about 3400 fibres.
It is the only nerve to decussate fully and emerge dorsally. (Last's p. 630)
Abducent nerve about 6600

The abducent nerve has about 6600 fibres.
It emerges at the lower border of the pons above the pyramid. (Last's p. 634-5)
Facial nerve about 7000

The facial nerve has about 7000 fibres.
They loop over the abducent nucleus at the facial colliculus. (Last's p. 635)
Receives preganglionic fibres through the nerve of the pterygoid canal

Greater petrosal fibres reach it through the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
They relay here and supply lacrimal, nasal and palatal glands. (Last's p. 635-6)
Is a relay for sympathetic fibres

Sympathetic (deep petrosal) fibres pass through without relaying.
So do taste fibres and maxillary sensory fibres. (Last's p. 635-6)
Supplies secretomotor fibres to the parotid

The parotid is supplied from the otic ganglion.
The pterygopalatine ganglion is "the ganglion of hay fever". (Last's p. 634)
Lies in the infratemporal fossa

It lies in the pterygopalatine fossa, hanging from the maxillary nerve.
The otic ganglion lies in the infratemporal fossa. (Last's)
Receives preganglionic fibres from the glossopharyngeal nerve

Its preganglionic fibres come from VII via the chorda tympani and lingual nerve.
The glossopharyngeal supplies the otic ganglion. (Last's p. 436)
Supplies the parotid gland

It supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands.
The parotid is supplied through the otic ganglion. (Last's)
Has preganglionic fibres from the inferior salivary nucleus

The fibres come from the superior salivary nucleus.
The inferior salivary nucleus belongs to IX. (Last's p. 436)
Hangs from the lingual nerve on hyoglossus

The ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve by two roots, on the surface of hyoglossus.
Postganglionic fibres pass to the gland and back to the lingual nerve. (Last's p. 461)
Passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

It emerges into the interpeduncular fossa and passes between these arteries.
An aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery can compress it. (Last's p. 606)
Lies highest in the lateral wall at the back of the cavernous sinus

III is highest posteriorly in the lateral wall; IV becomes uppermost anteriorly.
It then divides near the superior orbital fissure. (Last's p. 630)
Enters the orbit within the tendinous ring as superior and inferior divisions

Both divisions pass within the common tendinous ring with VI and nasociliary.
The superior division supplies superior rectus and levator. (Last's p. 632)
Has parasympathetic fibres that relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion

They relay in the ciliary ganglion.
Short ciliary nerves then supply sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. (Last's p. 607)
